I just tried to tag the definition of leftLim with to_dual but it doesn't work:

@[to_dual Function.rightLim]
noncomputable def Function.leftLim
    {α β : Type*} [LinearOrder α] [TopologicalSpace β] (f : α → β) (a : α) : β := by
  classical
  haveI : Nonempty β := ⟨f a⟩
  letI : TopologicalSpace α := Preorder.topology α
  exact if 𝓝[<] a = ⊥ ∨ ¬∃ y, Tendsto f (𝓝[<] a) (𝓝 y) then f a else limUnder (𝓝[<] a) f

gives

@[to_dual] failed. The translated value is not type correct. For help, see the docstring of `to_additive`, section `Troubleshooting`. Failed to add declaration
Function.rightLim:
Application type mismatch: The argument
  instBot
has type
  Bot (Filter α)
but is expected to have type
  Top (Filter α)
in the application
  @Top.top (Filter α) instBot

The reason is that it tries to translate the bot filter in the definition to the top filter, while it shouldn't. Is there a way to tell it not to translate this (or to declare the definition by hand and then tell to_dual to use it as the dualized version)?
I'm pretty sure there is, but don't know the right incantation. Is there to_dual_dont_translate? CC @Jovan Gerbscheid

I don't think this is supported at the moment: we want to dualize α, but not Filter α. There is @[to_dual (dont_translate := α)], but that is clearly not what you want here (and dont_translate only accepts names of local variables, not genereal expressions)
I tried attribute [to_dual_dont_translate] Filter and it seems to have fixed the problem
Yes, Aaron is right, you have to tag Filter with @[to_dual_dont_translate]

Indeed, it fixes the problem on translating the definition. Proving the next lemmas with @[to_dual] fails, though, I guess because of Preorder.topology α and OrderTopology α which to_dual doesn't know how to handle.
Yes, unfortuately we have to to to_dual tagging from the bottom up, because to_dual needs to know what to translate.

Aaron Liu said:

I tried attribute [to_dual_dont_translate] Filter and it seems to have fixed the problem

Does this interfere with translating between Filter.atTop and Filter.atBot, which we surely want to do in other places?
Oh, maybe that works correctly: we can translate particular operations on filters, we just don't want to translate anything to do with the order on filters.

Indeed, the to_dual_dont_translate tells to_dual to not translate orders on that type. But when translating atTop [Preorder α] : Filter α, to_dual checks whether it needs to translate the order on α, which typically willl not contain the type Filter.
In the same way, we can translate Set.Ioo, and Set is tagged with to_dual_dont_translate.
In fact, here's a PR that makes a start at tagging Filter.atTop with to_dual, and tags Filter with to_dual_dont_translate: #35133

Do we have a preference on whether we prefer to tag iSup stuff with @[to_dual] and delete iInf or the other way round?
docs#WithBot survived over docs#WithTop, but docs#iSup / docs#upperClosure survived over docs#iInf / docs#lowerClosure.
If there's a preference I do not know it. I've just been doing whatever is easiest with any given file.
We typically keep whichever is defined first. It would at least be nice to be consistent with such a choice.

/poll
Keep "top" / "sup" / "max" / "upper" / "lub" / "join" / ...
Keep "bot" / "inf" / "min" / "lower" / "glb" / "meet" / ...
We should be consistent but I don't have a preference
Author's choice per definition, no need for consistency
I think it's not clear in which list the glb/lub should go. Also, isn't bot the empty supremum? :upside_down:
I agree, but glb has "lower" similar to docs#LowerSet, and also docs#isLUB_iSup / docs#isGLB_iInf, so it seems to fit
Worth pointing out that in the docs, both versions of a theorem appear side by side. So all this really changes is which of the two appears first.
It does affect regex searches for theorems in the source code, and what people see when ctrl+clicking.

Yeah but the code still matters even if the docs are the same
FWIW I'm asking because I was about to write a new definition and I needed to make a choice
I would suggest to try to be as consistent as possible with what's already there. Consistency is always nice if it doesn't come at a cost.

I'm inclined to say that we should keep all the limit stuff, and generate all the colimit stuff with to_dual.
That's how most informal maths treats category theory (probably just because all the "co" would make the text longer??) and it seems this trend also happens in Mathlib.

So then, infima are limits, suprema are colimits. Etc...
Well, there are two ways to see a preorder as a category, and it depends on that choice what is a limit and what is a colimit :upside_down:

luckily mathlib instances have made that choice for us

import Mathlib

variable {α : Type*} [Preorder α]
open CategoryTheory

example (a b : α) : (a ≤ b) ≃ (a ⟶ b) where
  toFun := homOfLE
  invFun := leOfHom
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv h := homOfLE_leOfHom h
some of these things aren't obviously limits or colimits, what about lower and upper sets?

Is there a preference regarding using previous_lemma (α := αᵒᵈ) .. and adding the to_dual existing attribute vs just using to_dual? And should existing theorems shown via (α := αᵒᵈ) be deleted in favor of to_dual?
In the case of orders
Since the (α := αᵒᵈ) versions are often much terser than the proofs translated by to_dual, I was wondering if some performance argument would apply

Lua Viana Reis said:

And should existing theorems shown via (α := αᵒᵈ) be deleted in favor of to_dual?

Yes
(I also like to double-check the type matches- I first tag foo_max with to_dual which creates foo_min, then the existing foo_min complains so I rename it to foo_min', then I replace its body with foo_min with the params, and when it works I delete foo_min')
I think another option is to just add to_dual existing on the declaration to be removed, and if it does not complain the types should match
idk, to_dual existing can work even when to_dual on the original doesn't (unless it was fixed?), so I don't think it should be used for verification
#mathlib4 > MulAut and to_additive @ 💬 (to_additive shares machinery with to_dual AFAIK, so to_dual existing will act the same)

to_dual existing verifies that the types match, so yes you can use it to check this. But to_dual existing does not look at the value, so it is possible that to_dual fails where to_dual existing succeeds.

It is true that the proof generated by to_dual is typically longer than an OrderDual proof. But performance-wise, this is typically cancelled out by the fact that if you use to_dual, Lean only needs to elaborate one proof rather than two.
Yes, to_dual could fail, but just for double-checking it should suffice, right? And it seems a bit quicker than replacing the body and dealing with parameters (but that's my impression)

One thing that is easy to miss (and I often miss it myself) is that you should add (reorder := ...) when the explicit arguments are in a different order in the two declarations. This may not get caught by to_dual existing, because it tries to fill in the reorder argument automatically.
(deleted)
The proof is complex, so unless it is easy to diagnose I think I will leave it as is (without the dualized version)
In this case the WithBot.coe_biInf (α := αᵒᵈ) proof works, so I will probably just add it and mark as to_dual existing

Lua Viana Reis said:

Yes, to_dual could fail, but just for double-checking it should suffice, right? And it seems a bit quicker than replacing the body and dealing with parameters (but that's my impression)

It would be nice if the error message said

name has already been declared {and has the same type / but the type does not match}
(well, this particular message is not really about to_dual but about duplicated declarations in general)

When tagging things with to_dual, you need to first tag all of the prerequisite theorems/definitions with to_dual. In this case the error says something about WithTop.instInfSet, which hints at the fact that it still needs to be tagged with to_dual.
Yes, but it seems to be tagged as such. I could not find the untagged declaration
It looks to me like docs#WithTop.instInfSet is not tagged.
Ah, I am sorry, I had added the tag in my local copy (but it still didn't work). I think it would be more helpful to discuss it in a PR
